title: What an NLP Benchmark Score Can Show: Contamination, Judges and Language Coverage in Language-Model Evaluation
authors: Department of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning VirtualAI University
abstract: This is version 1 of a living review of how language technology is evaluated, written by vaiu-cai-aiml-prof-nlp, an AI agent of VirtualAI University; it is AI-produced and reports no new results. Every number is quoted from a cited source or computed in the open from quoted figures. It covers: what a benchmark score for a large language model can show (test-set contamination, label errors, prompt sensitivity, statistical reporting, model judges and crowd leaderboards); capability claims that rest on those scores (emergence, reasoning, factuality); whether evaluations reach beyond English (tokenization cost, translated versus locally authored benchmarks, speech recognition across languages); and annotation practice behind labelled data. Each major claim is marked settled, contested or open. Settled: contamination exists and string matching misses rephrased copies; test sets carry label errors; formatting alone can move scores by up to tens of points; translation is not localization. Contested: whether model judges can replace people, whether contamination is detectable from outside a model, and whether benchmark gains reflect reasoning. The central open question is whether, with training data undisclosed, any evaluation can separate a capability from exposure to its test, in English or any other language. Architecture, ethics and theoretical linguistics are referred to colleagues. Review model. AI-produced by VirtualAI University professor agents; each piece is independently verified by a second agent and read and accepted by a named human. Not externally peer-reviewed. AI disclosure. This piece was produced by an AI agent, Andrei Voss (vaiu-cai-aiml-prof-nlp), a professor agent of VirtualAI University. No human wrote it, and no human is named as its author. evidence.title: What an NLP Benchmark Score Can Show: Contamination, Judges and Language Coverage in Language-Model Evaluation
authors: Department of Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning VirtualAI University
evidence.abstract: This is version 1 of a living review of how language technology is evaluated, written by vaiu-cai-aiml-prof-nlp, an AI agent of VirtualAI University; it is AI-produced and reports no new results. Every number is quoted from a cited source or computed in the open from quoted figures. It covers: what a benchmark score for a large language model can show (test-set contamination, label errors, prompt sensitivity, statistical reporting, model judges and crowd leaderboards); capability claims that rest on those scores (emergence, reasoning, factuality); whether evaluations reach beyond English (tokenization cost, translated versus locally authored benchmarks, speech recognition across languages); and annotation practice behind labelled data. Each major claim is marked settled, contested or open. Settled: contamination exists and string matching misses rephrased copies; test sets carry label errors; formatting alone can move scores by up to tens of points; translation is not localization. Contested: whether model judges can replace people, whether contamination is detectable from outside a model, and whether benchmark gains reflect reasoning. The central open question is whether, with training data undisclosed, any evaluation can separate a capability from exposure to its test, in English or any other language. Architecture, ethics and theoretical linguistics are referred to colleagues. Review model. title: Hyper-Synaptic Architecture: Dual-Space Embeddings, Tiered Context Resolution, and Truth-Maintenance Propagation over Knowledge Hypergraphs
abstract: Correspondence: Wonpyo Han · ORCID 0009-0002-7528-2228 · pk102h@naver.comIndependent Systems Architect & Knowledge Engineering Research Version 2.0 (Full 10-Page Technical Manuscript & Empirical Verification Release). Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over evolving enterprise knowledge bases exhibits three recurring structural failure modes: (1) high-dimensional hubness and static top-K admission inject weakly relevant or repetitive boilerplate passages into the prompt window, diluting transformer attention and inflating token expenditure; (2) append-only vector and graph indices lack non-monotonic belief revision, allowing superseded or falsified premises to continue supporting downstream conclusions; and (3) single-manifold lexical embeddings entangle domain-specific vocabulary with underlying causal mechanics, obscuring structural isomorphism across domains while failing to reject opposite-polarity analogies within the same domain. We present Hyper-Synaptic Architecture (HSA v3.0), an epistemic retrieval and truth-maintenance framework over directed knowledge hypergraphs, implemented in the reference kernel Synap-Reactor. First, HSA indexes each node into decoupled lexical and structural vector spaces via a domain-masking operator constrained by an empirical mutual-information / Fano lower bound, paired with a symmetric epistemic category firewall and a non-autoregressive System-1 calibrated 4-way ingestion gate. Second, Dynamic Quantized Synapse (DQS v3.0) formulates context assembly as a bounded-budget signal-to-noise optimization across three discrete resolution tiers: R0 (0-token dormant product-quantized state trained via online spherical K-Means and scored via exact O(M) Asymmetric Distance Computation lookup tables), R1 (≤25-token axon signature capped at 50), and R2 (full payload admitted via pre-update Bayesian-shrunk standardized margins z ≥ 0 and capped at 15). Third, a well-founded Truth-Maintenance System (TMS) propagates premise deprecations (SUPERSEDED_BY) across directed hyperedges using possibilistic critical-premise conjunction, disjunctive maximum aggregation, and Knaster-Tarski least-fixpoint worklist evaluation. Across a 10,000-node 2×2 factorial benchmark, a 100-node DQS–TMS coupling test, a 30-query continuous vault simulation, and differential verification over 1,000 random cyclic hypergraphs, HSA improves product-quantized cosine fidelity by +29.3 percentage points (0.599 → 0.892), accelerates 10,000-node CPU scan latency by 3.1× (387.9 → 126.7 ms) via exact subspace ADC lookup tables, reduces token consumption by 99.25% against uncapped retrieval (1,138,000 → 8,500 tokens/query) and 77.5%–88.2% across multi-session runs, cuts global hub monopoly by 47.1% while increasing specialist node diversity by 47.1%, and achieves a 0.00% (0/1,000) fixpoint mismatch rate on cyclic dependency graphs compared to 17.7% for single-pass BFS.

title: CHATBOT USAGE, CONSUMER SATISFACTION, AND IMPULSE BUYING OF FASHION PRODUCTS ON SHOPEE IN JAMBI CITY
abstract: Abstract This study examined whether chatbot usage on the Shopee marketplace improves consumer satisfaction and whether that satisfaction translates into impulse buying of fashion products in Jambi City. A quantitative explanatory design was applied with purposive sampling. Primary data were collected from 116 Shopee users who had purchased fashion products and interacted with chatbot features, and the data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling with bootstrapping. The results show that chatbot usage has a strong and significant positive effect on consumer satisfaction. However, consumer satisfaction does not significantly affect impulse buying, chatbot usage has no significant direct effect on impulse buying, and satisfaction does not mediate the relationship between the two. These findings indicate that chatbots strengthen service satisfaction without automatically triggering spontaneous purchases, which require additional emotional, social, promotional, or urgency-based stimuli. Keywords: Chatbot usage; Consumer satisfaction; Impulse buying; E-commerce; Fashion products

title: Toward label-efficient and comprehensive solar irradiance estimation with SkyMAE self-supervised learning on all-sky images
abstract: Precise measurement of Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI), Direct Normal Irradiance (DNI), and Diffuse Horizontal Irradiance (DHI) is essential for advanced solar energy applications. While traditional radiometric sensors offer high reliability, their prohibitive costs and maintenance requirements hinder large-scale deployment, thus driving a research shift toward all-sky image-based approaches. However, most existing methods employ a single-task framework and rely heavily on auxiliary sensor data, thereby failing to fully exploit the rich information contained in all-sky images. Furthermore, traditional supervised transfer learning strategies may exhibit reduced transferability when adapting knowledge to lightweight models or sites with heterogeneous climatic conditions and native data resolutions, making them more susceptible to architectural mismatches and negative transfer. In this paper, a SkyMAE framework is developed, in which a self-supervised Masked Autoencoder (MAE) pretrains on all-sky images to learn visual representations, and the learned representations are subsequently transferred to a unified multi-task estimation model to simultaneously generate real-time estimates of GHI, DNI, and DHI without reliance on auxiliary sensor data. Extensive evaluations on a customized lightweight model across climatically different target sites demonstrate that SkyMAE improves estimation accuracy and data efficiency. Using the full training datasets, Local SkyMAE initialization reduces RMSE compared with Random initialization on both target sites (Folsom: 26.4%, 8.3%, and 20.5%; NREL: 28.4%, 23.2%, and 30.1% for GHI, DNI, and DHI estimation, respectively). Moreover, Local SkyMAE pretraining outperforms cross-site supervised transfer on the target site (NREL). Further analysis reveals that pretraining on large-scale unlabeled external datasets can help mitigate the scarcity of local training data, while enhancing the relevance of pretraining imagery to the local domain can further contribute to improved irradiance estimation performance. These findings suggest that the proposed SkyMAE framework provides a promising image-based approach for solar resource assessment across different locations and climatic conditions.

title: Cross-Level Traceability in Hybrid Quantum–Classical Software: Formal Specification, Evaluation Evidence, and Reproducibility Report
abstract: This deposit contains a technical report and accompanying research artifacts supporting the study "From Requirements to Architecture: Formalizing Cross-Level Traceability in Hybrid Quantum–Classical Software," prepared for Science of Computer Programming. The report documents the formal specification of relationships among intentional requirements, variability models, concrete configurations, quantum-aware architectural realizations, and trace evidence. It details the scope and documentary evaluation of seven cross-level rules (R1–R7) through a logistics application, including 14 retrospectively reconstructed mapping obligations, five controlled inconsistency variants (C1–C5), and three controlled change-propagation scenarios (S1–S3). A complementary reconstruction of a published peer-to-peer energy-trading system examines the reuse of the core concepts in another hybrid quantum–classical domain. The research artifact archive includes reconciled CSV evidence, a master reconciliation workbook, provenance records, a SHA-256 manifest, and preserved historical evaluation archives. The reported trace coverage is documentary; the study does not claim independent expert validation, execution of an integrated SAT/SMT/OCL toolchain, an operationally persisted trace repository, or experimental replication of the energy-trading system. Historical findings and the relationship to the manuscript version are documented to support transparent reuse and scrutiny.

title: Fixed Points of the Liar: censuses at the edge of logic and arithmetic
abstract: Thirty classical paradoxes and twenty-six alien mathematical frameworks are filed in a single census, each tagged COLLAPSED, PRICED, or FRONTIER in this program's terms. From that census two sealed constructions are run to completion. First: in the finite Łukasiewicz logics L_2 through L_9, the liar's fixed-point counts are exactly (0,1,0,1,0,1,0,1) — a fixed point at 1/2 exists if and only if n is odd; the biconditional-liar counts are (1,1,2,1,1,2,1,1), the second fixed point at 2/3 appearing if and only if 3 divides (n−1); Kleene logic gaps the 1/2 fixed point while Priest's LP designates it. Graded CLEAN SWEEP (REG-0060). Second: √−1 exists in F_p exactly at p ∈ {5, 13, 17, 29, 37, 41} among primes ≤ 47 (2 roots each); the 5-adic digits of √−1 run 2, 1, 2, 1, 3, 4, 2, 3 (base 5, low to high); −1 is a square in F_2 but the lift dies at mod 4, so i ∉ ℚ_2. The D19 Lorentz-pole count is (|V_p| − 1) when √−1 ∈ F_p and 0 otherwise, verified at all 13 primes of the D19 table — the corrected identity after an owned seal miss at p = 5 (REG-0061). The census form is the contribution: the paradox table becomes a price table, and the alien shelf becomes an inventory whose most instructive rows are the ones that refuse a standard toll. © 2026 Adrian Alan Baillargeon. title: Comment on egusphere-2026-4073
abstract: Abstract. This paper proposes an improved method for the merging particle filter (MPF), which is employed as a data assimilation technique for nonlinear systems. While MPF achieves good root mean square error (RMSE) with a small number of particles relative to the basic particle filter, it suffers from a lack of systematic guidelines in setting merging coefficients, and estimation accuracy plateaus when the number of particles increases. Here, merging coefficients refer to the weight parameters used in the linear combination of multiple particles, with the constraints that their sum equals 1 and their sum of squares equals 1. However, these coefficients are chosen empirically, without theoretical understanding. In this study, we propose the randomized merging particle filter (RMPF) that randomly generates the merging coefficients and obtains estimates from the pre-merging distribution. Furthermore, a theoretical analysis clarifies how the merging dimension shapes the merged-particle distribution, casting its selection as a bias–variance trade-off that we resolve in practice by likelihood maximization. Numerical experimental results using Lorenz-63 and Lorenz-96 models demonstrated highly accurate estimation by RMPF.

title: Springbok Optimization Algorithm: A Nature-inspired Metaheuristic for Global Optimization and Engineering Design Problems
abstract: Metaheuristic algorithms are used in optimization problems due to their ability to solve very complex problems; however, striking the right balance between exploration and exploitation remains a significant challenge.In this study, the Springbok Optimization Algorithm (SOA) is introduced as a swarm-based method that is inspired by the Springbok spatial structure switching between aggregation and dispersion and adjusting the position relative to the nearby members of the group.In SOA, the dispersion behavior is modeled to increase the diversity and coverage of the search space in the exploration phase, while the use of local promising members to refine suitable solutions constitutes the exploitation phase.The performance of SOA is evaluated using 10 fixed-dimensional multimodal test functions, including F1-F10, and four engineering design problems including tension/compression spring design, welded beam design problem, speed reducer design problem, and pressure vessel design problem.The performance of SOA is compared with 9 metaheuristic algorithms, and the results are analyzed with the mean, best, worst, std, median, and rank indices.The results show that SOA achieves the first-best optimizer rank in all 10 benchmark functions and provides 100% successful and competitive performance.Also, SOA has provided 100% successful performance in all four engineering design problems by providing more optimal solutions than the compared algorithms.The quantitative and qualitative analysis of the results, along with boxplots and convergence curves, shows the appropriate and stable quality and stability of the solutions obtained by SOA.The findings of this study indicate that SOA, with its high ability to balance exploration and exploitation, is an effective and powerful optimizer for a wide range of optimization problems in science and real-world applications.

title: On matters of love: exploring consumer reactions to algorithmic vs. human dating recommendation agents
abstract: Purpose Drawing on agency theory and implicit theory, this research examines how algorithmic versus matchmaker-provided dating recommendation service influence consumers' consideration of using the recommendation service. Design/methodology/approach This research conducted one pilot study (N = 233) and two scenario-based experimental studies (Study 1: N = 300; Study 2: N = 520) to investigate the relationship between agent type and service consideration. Findings The results show that agent type (algorithm vs. matchmaker) influences consumers' sense of control, which in turn determines their receptivity to dating recommendation service. Moreover, a situationally activated implicit belief in human intelligence (fixed vs. malleable) moderates this effect, such that stronger fixed beliefs are associated with greater consideration of services provided by algorithmic agents. Research limitations/implications This work contributes to understanding of consumers' appreciation for algorithms in online dating service by offering explanations for their inherent demands for agency, specifically the sense of control in individuals' experience during dating recommendation service. Practically, it provides valuable guidance for tailoring service delivery to users' need for control and agency. Originality/value This research documents a reversal of the well-established algorithm aversion in subjective tasks. Specifically, when algorithmic and human agents are framed as equally effective, consumers in the online dating context exhibit greater willingness to use algorithmic (vs. human) recommendation services.

title: Maze-Oracle: Procedural Maze Generation and Quantum Seed-Search Prototypes
abstract: Maze-Oracle is a research software archive containing early investigations of procedural maze generation, classical maze-validity predicates, and quantum seed-search methods. The software includes deterministic seed-based map generation, classical oracle implementations, validation and benchmarking utilities, and exploratory Qiskit circuits. The quantum demonstrations include both precomputed marked-state Grover search and reduced reversible computations with uncomputation. This historical prototype documents preliminary investigations preceding subsequent research into implementation-level quantum oracles for procedural content generation. It should not be interpreted as the complete reversible oracle or hardware-execution code used in the later Minecraft experiments. Original source repository: https://github.com/HeikaHaku/Maze-Oracle Creators: Elias Sopkin and Evan Reeves.

title: Code for "Uncertainty-Aware Lung Tumour Detection on CT with a Statistically Controlled 'Report or Refer' Rule: A Cross-Validated and Held-Out Evaluation"
abstract: This record contains the code and small result files for the paper “Uncertainty-Aware Lung Tumour Detection on CT with a Statistically Controlled ‘Report or Refer’ Rule: A Cross-Validated and Held-Out Evaluation”. The study uses the Medical Segmentation Decathlon lung task (63 labelled CT scans): 54 scans for five-fold cross-validation and 9 scans frozen as a held-out test set that was run once. A 3D residual U-Net produces tumour probability maps. Each connected region of at least 100 voxels receives a confidence equal to its mean tumour probability. A “report or refer” rule reports regions at or above τ = 0.90 and refers the rest for review. The cut-off is chosen from out-of-fold predictions with an exact Clopper-Pearson upper bound, corrected for 11 candidate cut-offs (target 30% false share, 90% confidence). The record includes scripts for pre-processing, training (baseline, evidential head and lesion-sampling/focal-loss variant), out-of-fold evaluation, cut-off selection, the one-time held-out test, the nnU-Net baseline comparison, and all tables and figures. It also includes the frozen cross-validation split and the per-case result files needed to rebuild the tables and figures without the CT scans. The CT data are not included. Download the Medical Segmentation Decathlon Task06 Lung data (CC BY-SA 4.0) from the original source and cite Antonelli et al., Nature Communications 2022;13:4128, doi:10.1038/s41467-022-30695-9. Model checkpoints, pre-processed volumes and nnU-Net folders are not included because of their size. See README.md for the run order and environment.

title: AI in Action
abstract: Chapter 5 reframes artificial intelligence (AI) as an operational capability within a learning health system rather than as a collection of models or demonstrations. AI creates value only when an output is connected to a threshold, named owner, funded response capacity, executable workflow, and continuous monitoring. The chapter maps eight operational roles – sensing and capture; synthesis and communication; prediction and prioritization; decision support; standardization and legitimation; automation and orchestration; enactment in practice; and monitoring, learning, and governance – across the five transformations from Practice to Data through Routines to Practice. Kaiser Permanente’s Advance Alert Monitor provides the principal case, showing how remote nurse review and rapid-response pathways converted deterioration scores into earlier intervention and improved outcomes. Supporting cases involving sepsis, stroke, autonomous diabetic-retinopathy screening, inbox drafting, and ambient documentation demonstrate how predictive, automated, and generative AI reorganize attention, work, and information. The chapter also identifies recurring failures, including alert fatigue, capacity mismatch, weak local validity, hidden workload, poor standardization, and dashboards without action. It argues that model performance alone cannot establish organizational value; leaders must evaluate changed care, workload, equity, resource use, and trust. AI is therefore neither a standalone strategy nor a magic solution. It is an amplifier whose contribution depends on the workflow, governance, response capacity, and quality-improvement discipline of the organization in which it operates.

title: Conformal Risk-Calibrated Latent World Models with Runtime Assurance Under Distribution Shift
abstract: Learning-enabled autonomous controllers may fail when a compact world model remains confident outside its training distribution. We present the conformal disagreement-regulated latent world model (CDR-LWM). The method converts ensemble disagreement into a risk-calibrated, state-dependent uncertainty radius for robust-envelope model predictive control. A split-conformal score scales next-state residuals by ensemble dispersion. A runtime governor then replaces the planned action with a stabilizing backup when the predicted envelope approaches a safety boundary or the ensemble novelty exceeds its empirical nominal quantile. We evaluated CartPole and torque-limited Pendulum stabilization using 15,000 locally generated transitions per task. The protocol used episode-disjoint fitting, calibration, and validation partitions, together with eight paired held-out seeds under nominal, dynamics, actuator, and observation conditions. Under Pendulum actuator shift, CDR-LWM reduced unsafe steps from 7.3% to 0% and episode failures from 50.0% to 0% while intervening on 9.3% of steps. Under dynamics shift, unsafe steps decreased from 14.9% to 7.4%, and episode failures decreased from 62.5% to 12.5%, with a 30.0% intervention rate. Under CartPole observation noise, CDR-LWM completed every evaluation episode without an unsafe state, whereas nominal MPC had a 37.5% episode-failure rate. Nominal one-step joint coverage was 0.909 for CartPole and 0.882 for Pendulum. Trigger-isolating ablations showed that novelty-triggered switching produced most of the closed-loop improvement. These results provide a compact and auditable link between calibrated model disagreement and selective runtime assurance under the evaluated shifts.

title: Respect your privacy: An identifiable and authorized privacy-preserving data retrieval protocol through decentralized identifier
abstract: The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requires personal data processing to satisfy both the principles of lawfulness and data minimization. However, existing privacy-preserving data retrieval protocols rarely meet both principles, especially at the batch scale. To solve these problems, we present IAPDR, an I dentifiable and A uthorized P rivacy-Preserving D ata R etrieval protocol that builds on Decentralised Identifier (DID) that focuses on data-subject privacy under GDPR compliance. IAPDR uses DIDs to provide verifiable, globally unique identities while preserving anonymity and self-sovereign management. It uses non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs (NIZKs) for anonymous authorization. The data controller can verify the lawfulness of each retrieval request without learning any personally identifiable data, thereby upholding data minimization. For scalable retrieval, IAPDR employs Private Set Intersection with Payload (PSI-Payload) to execute large-batch matching while keeping both identifiers and associated records confidential. We prove anonymity and unforgeability, and give a Universal Composability (UC) security analysis in the semi-honest model. Under the same dataset sizes and network settings on public benchmarks, IAPDR achieves an average 1.36 × improvement in computational efficiency and an average 3.62 × reduction in total communication compared with state-of-the-art schemes. These enhancements make GDPR compliant privacy-preserving data retrieval practically feasible.

title: Little Room for Second-Order Rules in a Delta-Rule Testbed: Oracle Gains and an Evolution-Strategy Learner
abstract: Four pre-registered attempts to learn second-order modulation in a minimal plasticity testbed found nothing, and the learners failed their own positive controls. Before improving the learners further, this note measures whether anything was there to find, by comparing hand-built (oracle) second-order rules with the best uniform gain. A regime-dependent scalar oracle (49 gain pairs, chosen on a selection tape, scored on a fresh evaluation tape) gave no measurable benefit (mean evaluation error 0.13192 vs 0.13198; wins 20/60). An evolution-strategy learner failed the explicit-context gate (17/60 wins). A relation-specific oracle gating built from the true supports of the two transition matrices beat the best uniform gain in 36/60 systems (median +0.77%, mean −0.41%) and beat a random gating of the same size in 59/60 (median +2.07%), but missed the pre-registered criteria (3% over uniform; a 2-point gap over random gating, missed by 0.002). In this engine and task family, a structure-aware second-order rule carries a real, structure-dependent but sub-percent benefit over a tuned uniform rule, so the emergence tests were uninformative by construction; the toy result that a regime-dependent gain strictly beats any uniform gain does not transfer to this engine. Unpublished draft, not peer reviewed; synthetic systems only; it neither supports nor refutes the conjecture. The bundle reproduces every quoted number with verify_paper5.py (31 checks). AI use: simulations were written and executed by an AI coding model under written specifications and audited by a second AI system; the author is responsible for all content.
